title: PPI Report Reality Check And Why November’s Calm H...
content:
PPI Report Reality Check And Why November’s Calm Headline Is Hiding Growing Economic Strain
The November PPI report doesn’t look dramatic. Headline final demand prices rose 0.2% month over month. If you stop there, it’s easy to conclude inflation is contained and the system is behaving.
But that headline hides where the pressure actually is.
What’s Driving The Number
Most of the move came from goods prices, which jumped 0.9% the biggest monthly increase in nearly two years. A large chunk of that was energy. Final demand energy prices rose 4.6%, with gasoline up more than 10% in a single month. That alone explains a meaningful share of the headline increase.
Meanwhile, services prices were flat. That divergence matters. It tells you this wasn’t broad based pricing power across the economy. it was a cost shock hitting specific inputs.
Strip out food, energy, and trade services, and core PPI was up 0.2% on the month and 3.5% year over year. That’s still elevated, but it’s not accelerating. It’s steady pressure, not runaway inflation.
Margins Are Getting Squeezed
The most important part of this report isn’t the headline. It’s trade services.
Wholesale and retail margins fell 0.8% in November, the largest drop since April. That means businesses weren’t able to pass higher costs through cleanly. They absorbed them.
This is how stress usually shows up before it hits growth or jobs. Not through collapsing demand, but through thinner margins. Companies discount. They compete harder. They protect volume instead of profit.
You can have inflation still running around 3% year over year and still have an economy that’s quietly losing pricing power.
Upstream vs. Downstream Tells the Same Story
Intermediate demand prices rose 0.3%, with processed goods up 0.6% and unprocessed goods up 0.4%. Energy again did most of the work. On a year over year basis, the earliest stage of production is still running hot..Stage 1 prices are up 3.7%, the fastest pace since early 2023.
That means costs are still moving through the pipeline.
But downstream, margins are narrowing. That gap of rising inputs, contested pricing is classic late cycle behavior.
What This Is (And Isn’t)
Producer prices are still rising year over year. Demand hasn’t collapsed. But it’s also not confirming a clean disinflation narrative.
Instead, it shows an economy where…
•   input costs can still spike suddenly,
•   consumers are more price sensitive,
•   and businesses are absorbing volatility rather than passing it on.
That’s not a healthy expansion phase. It’s a balancing act.
My View
The PPI isn’t telling you inflation is back. It’s telling you inflation is uneven, and the burden of adjustment is shifting onto corporate margins.
That’s usually how the cycle turns. Not with a crash in prices, but with companies losing room to maneuver. When margins compress long enough, hiring slows, capex gets cautious, and growth cools without a headline moment.
This print looks calm on the surface. Underneath, it’s signaling an economy that’s still under pressure..just in subtler, more uncomfortable ways.

title: January 2026 Beige Book Looks Stable On The Surfac...
content:
January 2026 Beige Book Looks Stable On The Surface But Fragile Underneath
8 of 12 districts reported “slight to modest” growth, 3 were flat, and only 1 saw a modest decline. That’s technically an improvement from recent cycles where “little change” dominated. But the details tell a more conditional story.  
Where The Growth Is Coming From
Most of the momentum came from holiday related consumer spending, and even that was uneven..
•   Spending was strongest among higher income households, especially on luxury goods, travel, and experiences.
•   Low and moderate income consumers were increasingly price sensitive, hesitating on nonessential purchases.
•   Auto sales were flat to down across most districts.
•   Manufacturing was split: 5 districts expanding, 6 contracting.
That’s not broad based strength. It’s a narrow pocket of resilience.
Labor Is Stable, but Defensive
Employment was described as “mostly unchanged”..
•   8 of 12 districts reported no net hiring growth.
•   When firms hired, it was mostly to backfill, not expand.
•   Multiple districts reported increased use of temporary workers “to stay flexible in uncertain times.”
•   Wage growth was moderate and back to pre pandemic norms, not accelerating.
One concrete data point cuts through the language: in Minneapolis, job postings fell 18% year over year. That’s not collapse..but it’s cooling.
Prices and Tariffs And The Margin Squeeze
Prices were said to be rising at a moderate pace, but tariffs were a consistent pressure across districts..
•   Firms that had been absorbing tariff costs are now passing them through as pre tariff inventories run out.
•   At the same time, retailers and restaurants are reluctant to raise prices because customers are price sensitive.
•   Energy and insurance costs were repeatedly cited as margin stressors.
This is the key tension..costs are rising faster than many businesses can pass them on.
Examples from districts..
•   Boston reported credit card processing fees up to 4%, with some merchants eating the cost.
•   St. Louis and Cleveland noted restaurants unable to pass costs along, leading to financial strain.
•   Dallas data showed manufacturing input costs averaged 5.5% in 2025, while selling prices rose only 2.3%.
That gap is where slowdowns usually start.
Consumers: K Shaped and Cautious
Across districts, the same pattern showed up..
•   Higher income consumers kept spending.
•   Middle and lower income households were trading down, comparing prices, and cutting discretionary spending.
•   In Cleveland, nearly 70% of low income workers said expenses rose, about half said income didn’t cover costs, and 45% planned to look for new jobs.
That’s pressure, not confidence.
My View
The Beige Book isn’t describing a confident expansion. It’s an economy that’s still moving, but on thinner margins and narrower demand.
The risk here isn’t a sudden break. It’s a grind..
•   rising input costs,
•   delayed price pass through,
•   margin compression,
•   cautious hiring,
•   and increasingly selective consumers.
That’s how growth slows quietly without a headline moment and the Beige Book, despite its calm tone, is already sketching that outline.

title: If Trump’s objective is to extend and entrench U.S...
content:
If Trump’s objective is to extend and entrench U.S. dollar dominance his public behavior since returning to office in 2025 including repeatedly and publicly asking Powell to cut rates looks contradictory at first glance…let me ask some questions that some of you on here can probably answer…
👇
Why publicly demand rate cuts while pursuing policies that are inflationary in the short term?
If tariffs raise input costs and push prices higher in the near term, that gives the Fed a textbook reason not to cut. Expecting Powell to ease into policy driven inflation contradicts basic central bank logic, unless the demand itself is performative rather than sincere.
Why push rate cuts when high rates strain dollar denominated debt globally?
Elevated rates increase servicing costs on trillions in offshore dollar debt, pushing borrowers toward distress and dependence on U.S.-controlled liquidity. Cutting rates would ease that pressure, reducing desperation and weakening the dollar’s coercive leverage.
Why advocate cuts that would flood global markets with liquidity and accelerate de dollarization?
Abundant, cheap dollars lower the need to hoard reserves, making it easier for BRICS nations to settle trade outside the dollar system. Scarcity does the opposite, it reinforces dependence and slows alternatives.
Why call for easing while expanding sanctions that restrict dollar access?
Sanctions weaponize the dollar by limiting access and forcing adversaries to negotiate from weakness. Rate cuts would partially offset that pressure, offering unintended relief and dulling sanctions’ effectiveness as a leverage tool.
Why push cuts and ease conditions for European banks facing dollar funding stress?
European banks USD mismatches create leverage for the U.S. via swap lines during crises. Cutting rates relieves that stress, reducing reliance on U.S. liquidity and diminishing bargaining power.
Why push cuts amid rising geopolitical tension?
Geopolitical stress boosts dollar demand as a safe haven, allowing the U.S. to extract concessions in exchange for liquidity access. Flooding the system with dollars weakens that leverage.
Why advocate easing as BRICS advances alternative payment rails like BRICS Pay?
These systems gain traction when dollars are abundant and cheap. Scarcity forces continued reliance on the existing dollar network.
Why call for lower rates despite warnings about growing USD funding mismatches abroad?
Such mismatches create pressure points the U.S. can exploit during liquidity crises. Easing relieves the squeeze, reducing dependence and limiting policy concessions in return.

title: CPI Report And What the Headline Misses
content:
CPI Report And What the Headline Misses
This December 2025 report has a structural issue that’s hard to ignore. The BLS notes that October and November 2025 values are missing due to a lapse in appropriations, and you can see the gaps where those months should appear in the tables and charts. CPI is a time series measure. Seasonal adjustment, trend interpretation, and momentum all assume continuity. A gap doesn’t imply manipulation, but it does reduce confidence in short term readings. You still see the year end picture, but you lose clarity on how the economy actually moved into it.
Stepping back, here’s what the report says in plain terms…
•   Headline CPI-U: +0.3% seasonally adjusted in December; +2.7% YoY
•   Core CPI (ex food & energy): +0.2% MoM; +2.6% YoY
•   Shelter: +0.4% MoM; +3.2% YoY, with OER and rent both +0.3%
•   Food: +0.7% MoM, with food at home and away from home rising
•   Energy: +0.3% MoM overall, gasoline down while utilities especially natural gas service jump
That’s the surface view. What matters is the composition underneath it.
Inflation Is Narrow Shelter and Food Are Carrying It
The anatomy of the +0.3% monthly print is telling. Shelter rose 0.4%, food rose 0.7%, and core inflation was only 0.2%. The report explicitly states shelter was the largest contributor.
When inflation is this concentrated, the question shifts. It’s no longer is inflation hot? but is inflation being held up by lagging categories while the rest of the economy cools? 
Shelter is a classic lagger. OER and rent often stay firm well after market rents and housing activity slow. That means CPI can look resilient even as real time demand weakens underneath it.
Goods Prices Are Losing Power
Outside of shelter, the goods side looks increasingly soft…
•   Used cars and trucks: −1.1% MoM
•   Lodging away from home: +2.9% MoM (volatile)
•   Communication: −1.9% MoM
•   Household furnishings and operations: down
•   Several tech and discretionary categories: declining
Core goods inflation excluding food and energy is running around 1.4% YoY, barely above zero.
That’s a familiar late cycle pattern. Discretionary demand fades first. Retailers discount. Pricing power erodes quietly before it shows up in labor or output data.
Services Are Sticky, Not Strong
Food inflation reaccelerating at +0.7% MoM isn’t demand strength, it’s cost pressure. At the same time, services inflation outside shelter remains firm…
•   Medical care services: +3.5% YoY
•   Hospital services: +6.6% YoY
•   Insurance: elevated
•   Transportation services: uneven and volatile
This is inflation in categories consumers can’t easily avoid, not inflation driven by growth.
Utilities Matter More Than Gasoline
Energy is split…
•   Gasoline: down MoM and YoY
•   Electricity and utility gas service: up meaningfully YoY
Utilities behave like a tax..sticky, unavoidable, and politically sensitive. Falling gasoline prices don’t offset rising utility bills. This pressure quietly compresses discretionary spending rather than triggering immediate CPI relief.
Chained CPI Shows Household Adaptation
Chained CPI rose 2.5% YoY, below CPI-U at 2.7% YoY.
That gap reflects substitution. Households aren’t spending more, they’re adjusting what they buy. That’s consistent with a late cycle consumer becoming more price sensitive, not a reaccelerating economy.
My View
This CPI report doesn’t read like an inflation resurgence, and it doesn’t suggest the data is broken. It reads like a late cycle setup…
•   Inflation held up by lagging shelter math
•   Goods demand weakening
•   Services inflation sticky because it’s unavoidable
•   Consumers adapting rather than expanding
If a downturn emerges, it likely won’t arrive through a dramatic CPI collapse. It shows up first in the quiet places..discretionary demand, credit quality, and CPI categories that stop moving because buyers simply disappear.

title: A big chunk of Canada’s real estate investment wor...
content:
A big chunk of Canada’s real estate investment world has quietly moved into defense mode. Funds managing roughly $30 billion including names like Centurion Apartment REIT and Trez Capital have been gating redemptions for the past couple of years. In plain terms, investors can’t get their money out on demand anymore. Not because managers want to trap capital, but because the market underneath them stopped cooperating.
The root cause isn’t mysterious. Rate hikes in 2022 and 2023 crushed the math. Borrowing costs jumped, transaction volumes dried up, and prices rolled over roughly an 18% drop from peak levels. At the same time, commercial real estate investment is down more than 20%, development pipelines have stalled, and construction loans..once treated as short duration and liquid are now anything but.
Why Gates Are Legal And Why They’re Being Used
These funds aren’t breaking rules. Their documents explicitly allow gates during periods of stress, and regulators permit it for a reason. If redemptions were honored in full right now, managers would be forced to dump properties or loans into a weak market, locking in losses for everyone who stays. Gating is meant to slow that process, spread the pain more evenly, and avoid fire sale dynamics.
This is less about protecting managers and more about preventing a classic liquidity mismatch from blowing up. Long dated, rate sensitive assets funded by investors who suddenly want cash don’t coexist peacefully when prices are falling.
The Deeper Problem Beneath The Surface
The uncomfortable part is what this signals about confidence. Nearly 40% of Canada’s private real estate fund market is now gated. That changes investor psychology. Capital gets cautious. New inflows slow. Recovery takes longer..especially for housing supply, which already depends heavily on continuous financing.
Funds are staring down a familiar spiral..redemptions force sales, sales push prices lower, lower prices hit NAVs, leverage ratios rise, lenders tighten, and suddenly a liquidity problem becomes a solvency conversation. In debt heavy real estate structures, that shift can happen faster than most expect.
The gates aren’t the crisis. They’re the tell. They’re a sign the system is under strain, and managers are buying time in a market that no longer forgives leverage, duration, or optimistic exit assumptions.
Canadian real estate funds worth $22 billion aren't letting investors withdraw their money, as property prices fall https://t.co/aouV8WsaSE

title: The Housing Shortage Narrative Is a Distraction Fr...
content:
The Housing Shortage Narrative Is a Distraction From Opportunity Scarcity
The darkest reds, shortages north of 15% of existing stock cluster exactly where you’d expect..Los Angeles County, the New York City boroughs, Miami-Dade. These are the economic magnets. Jobs, capital, services, and population keep flowing in, so housing gets tight fast. Meanwhile, huge parts of the Midwest, rural South, and interior West are pale or even blue, signaling little shortage or outright surplus. That contrast matters. It tells you this isn’t a uniform national problem, it’s a geographic concentration problem.
The danger is in how that gets framed. When people say “America has a housing shortage,” it sounds like we’re short everywhere. The map shows something very different..we’re short where growth is concentrated and oversupplied where people are leaving.
The Japan Parallel Hiding In Plain Sight
Japan offers a clean preview of how this dynamic can play out. As its population peaked around 128 million and began declining..falling below 125 million by the mid 2020s the pain didn’t hit evenly. Young people moved to Tokyo, Osaka, and a few other hubs. Rural towns emptied out. By the 2020s, Japan had roughly 9 million vacant homes, mostly outside major cities. Urban areas faced real housing pressure and soaring prices, while the countryside was drowning in surplus.
The response wasn’t to prop up every shrinking village. Japan shifted to what they called “smart shrinkage” consolidating schools, hospitals, and infrastructure in places where people and productivity still clustered. Funding quietly moved toward urban cores. The public justification was often urban housing shortages or affordability crises..even though, nationally, housing wasn’t scarce at all. It was misallocated.
Why This Matters For The U.S.
Now look back at the U.S. map. We’re not shrinking nationally yet, but the pattern is forming. Birth rates are below replacement. The population is aging. Immigration keeps totals stable, but it’s uneven..flowing into a handful of metros tied to tech, finance, and services. Those red counties are magnets in the same way Tokyo was.
The political language is starting to rhyme. “National housing shortage” becomes the justification for zoning changes, subsidies, and incentives that mostly benefit high density urban cores. Meanwhile, rural counties and older industrial regions keep losing people, tax base, and services. Schools consolidate. Hospitals close. Infrastructure decays. Eventually, policymakers call it efficiency. 
The Deeper Implication
This isn’t really about building everywhere. It’s about deciding where the future is allowed to concentrate. The housing shortage narrative keeps the focus on construction in cities, but underneath it’s preparing the ground for managed contraction elsewhere. Over the next few decades, it’s not hard to imagine hundreds of U.S. counties drifting toward the Japanese model..cheap, empty housing, shrinking services, and quiet abandonment while a few metros grow denser, richer, and more politically powerful.
It may be pragmatic in a world of uneven population growth. But it also means the winners and losers are being locked in geographically. And once that shift starts, it’s very hard to reverse.
The U.S. housing shortage mapped by county
This map shows estimated housing shortages across U.S. counties, assuming a nationwide shortfall of roughly six million homes. Shortage here is expressed as a share of existing housing stock, allowing differences between large urban counties and smaller rural ones to be compared on the same scale.
Source: AEI Housing Center, Housing Shortage Toolkit (https://t.co/KlKF9KAPqB)

title: On a very long term monthly view, NDX is pressing ...
content:
On a very long term monthly view, NDX is pressing into a zone that’s acted like a ceiling before. It’s sitting at the top of a rising channel that’s been in place since the late ’80s, right where a major long run extension level lines up. We saw a similar everything converges here moment near the dot com peak..not because markets obey magic numbers, but because extreme positioning and long trends tend to show up at obvious reference points.
This isn’t about precision. It’s about context. When price gets this extended relative to its own history, upside doesn’t usually vanish but it does stop being easy.
Why The Macro Backdrop Matters More This Time
Taking the broader data into account actually sharpens the point. The stress building underneath this market isn’t a 2008 style housing collapse, it’s a refinancing, unsecured consumer, and CRE squeeze, and that distinction matters for how this resolves.
Auto delinquencies aren’t a little high. The 60 day rate is around 1.54%, with subprime already worse than GFC. Credit card delinquencies are roughly 2.98% entering 2026 basically GFC adjacent. Student loans are the sleeper issue..about 8.8 million borrowers, nearly 1 in 4 are already in default, with delinquencies projected toward 39%  by year end. That’s a consumer balance sheet fracture, it just isn’t showing up in mortgages the way it did in 2008.
CRE is even more direct. Office vacancies are running 19%-20%, with some forecasts pushing toward 24%, and CMBS office delinquencies are 11.3% to 11.8%, already above the GFC peak of roughly 10.7%. That’s not the cycle is fine. That’s collateral impairment.
Layer on the maturity wall…9 trillion dollars of U.S. marketable debt rolling in 2026 refinancing closer 4%-5%, plus about $936 billion in CRE maturities next year and over $1.5 trillion including the 2025 backlog and you can see why term premium wants to rise. The supply and refinancing impulse is real.
What I Think Comes Next
This is where the chart and the macro intersect. In a stable economy, cuts that look fiscally accommodative can push the long end higher. But in a world where consumer credit and CRE are actively cracking, there’s a very plausible path where that doesn’t happen because a tightening credit impulse overwhelms the fiscal narrative and forces a dash for collateral. That’s the scenario where long rates fall anyway, even if the fiscal story is ugly.
So I don’t think this has to be a straight replay of 2000. Today’s index is full of real businesses with real cash flow. But I do think we’re at the part of the cycle where returns get paid in volatility, not smooth upside. In my opinion this is a regime shift toward mean reversion, with the 2022 highs as the first real gravity level if the macro narrative cracks.
This is usually the phase where belief alone stops working. The trend doesn’t end all at once, it just starts charging a much higher price for staying in it.

Of course It coincides perfectly with the tap and rejection at channel top - a channel which had a trajectory formed very early on with the 86 & 88 lows. Nevertheless, if we retrace the 82% that the 2000 did, then, get this...it takes us just about down retest that high...Fibs are fun, no?

title: Rick Rieder isn’t an academic or a headline econom...
content:
Rick Rieder isn’t an academic or a headline economist…he’s a markets person who’s spent his entire career watching where things actually break. At BlackRock, he runs global fixed income and sits at the center of rates, credit, and multi asset allocation decisions that move trillions. Before that, he came up through Lehman Brothers and later founded R3 Capital during the financial crisis, which BlackRock acquired. That matters because his instincts were forged in moments when liquidity disappears and refinancing risk suddenly becomes the story.
He’s known less for grand theories and more for understanding transmission and how policy decisions flow through funding markets, credit spreads, housing, and the cost of capital. He’s the kind of investor who cares whether the pipes are shaking, not whether the model looks clean.
Where He Stands On Policy And Why It Resonates Now
On monetary policy, Rieder tends to be pragmatic. He’s generally argued that once rates cross from restrictive into outright constrictive, they start doing damage..especially to housing, small businesses, and credit!dependent parts of the economy. That’s why he’s been more open than many to rate cuts in this phase of the cycle. Not because easy money is good, but because tightening into a refinancing wall is how accidents happen.
On fiscal policy, he’s more measured. You don’t hear him cheering deficits, but you do hear him acknowledge reality that when debt loads are large, the cost of capital matters enormously. His focus is usually on whether policy..monetary or fiscal is making the system more fragile at the margin.
On crypto, his tone has been unusually sober for someone from traditional fixed income. He’s described Bitcoin as durable, has compared it favorably to gold as a store of value, and has treated it as something that belongs in modern portfolios..not as a trade, but as a structural asset. That’s less about hype and more about recognizing how markets evolve.
Why His Name Keeps Coming Up
It’s not hard to see why someone like Trump would be drawn to Rieder. Trump has always favored operators over bureaucrats, people who’ve run real money and understand markets from the inside. Rieder fits that mold..a Wall Street winner, comfortable with scale, and openly critical of policy staying too tight for too long. Picking someone like him would signal a shift toward growth first thinking while still giving markets a sense of credibility.
The bigger point, though is Rieder’s speciality is management during times of stress. He’s spent decades managing through moments when credit turns, liquidity dries up, and policy mistakes get exposed. In a cycle where refinancing risk, credit strain, and term premium are quietly becoming the main characters, that skill set suddenly looks very relevant.
